story|title:an indic voice agent with cu.content_excerpt: Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type. We built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps . A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent: If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up. CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things: The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it. Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server. Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval : a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph. Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly says "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning. The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large ), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything. story|title:belay deterministic semantic.content_excerpt: Semantic diffs, integrity checks and receipts for what agents change on a system. Pre-alpha. Intent: record what changed on a system, explain it in semantic terms rather than as a path list, and make it reversible. Status: pre-alpha. The checkpoint and diff engine runs (below); the formats it writes are drafts that may still change, and the latest pre-release is v0.1.0-alpha.11. Nothing that changes your files exists yet. Pre-alpha. The most useful contribution right now is real-world use. Run belay around something you actually do (an agent session, a build, an install) and compare its report with what really happened. If it missed a change, invented one, or buried the real change in noise, open an issue with the receipt. That's the data I need the most. No commit , discard , restore or undo: belay records and explains, and changes nothing. The session engine under src/session/ (namespaces and overlays) is not part of the belay binary. No stable release. Today belay only records and reports; it contains nothing. The session engine, when it ships, is meant as a safety boundary, not a security boundary — built for accidents, not for hostile code; it will not contain a process that is actively trying to escape. See SECURITY.md . What a checkpoint does not see: anything outside the scope, anything below a mount point inside it, belay's own state directory and the paths you exclude (left out, and named in every manifest), and network effects (pushes, API calls, emails). On filesystems with coarse timestamps some same-size rewrites can be missed; the limits are in docs/spec/manifest-v1.md . A file being written while it is read is marked and reported unknown where the kernel can say so, and counted where it can't ( docs/cli.md ). make needs a C11 compiler and GNU make, on Linux or macOS; make check also needs python3. The binary is bin/belay . Apache-2.0. The core stays Apache-2.0, permanently. If paid offerings ever exist they will be separate products — never features removed from or withheld by this repository. story|title:do inconsistent docs hurt ai.content_excerpt: Every product’s docs drift out of step with the product. A product that’s been around for years has pages written against features that have since changed, and each change reaches only the pages someone remembers to update. A product that’s moving fast, as many are today with AI, drifts even sooner. An endpoint gets renamed or a setting moves, and the reference gets updated while a how-to or a sample keeps the old value. Before long, two of your pages tell the reader two different things. When developers hit two pages that disagree, they usually find out which one is right the hard way. They copy the code from one page, run it and watch it fail. Every minute they then put into working out which page to trust goes into debugging your docs. Coding agents read the same pages, so we wanted to know how they handle a contradiction. Does an agent notice that two pages disagree? If it follows the wrong one, does it recover and pay for the detour in tokens, or does it get stuck and hand back something that doesn’t work? And if the result is broken, does the agent tell you? We tested three contradictions that had been live in a product’s docs, with three models and about 140 agent runs. Agents often noticed that two pages disagreed, and still followed the wrong page first. When the mistake broke something the agent could see, like an API call that returned a 404, every agent recovered, but the detour added as much as 38% to the tokens it used. When the mistake stayed silent until CI, an agent sometimes handed back a broken result and told the user the work was done. Agents that checked a second source before writing code weren’t misled at all. The three contradictions came from the docs of Dev Proxy , an API simulator that developers use to mock APIs and test how their apps handle errors. We needed contradictions that had been live in real docs, with a known right answer, and Dev Proxy has the history that produces them. Dev Proxy went from v0.29 to v4.0 in about a year and a half, and each major version left behind pages written for the one before. A consistency review of its documentation on Microsoft Learn pulled 3,827 facts out of the pages and found 79 places where two pages disagreed. We’ve since fixed most of them, so for every contradiction we had the page from before the fix and the same page after it. story|title:finding faster quantum algor.content_excerpt: How using agent teams and formal verification can improve quantum algorithms for modelling fusion energy, chemistry and enzymes Quantum computers could soon solve problems beyond the reach of classical supercomputers. However, there is a catch: even when using the best quantum algorithms, some important applications still require more resources than early quantum hardware will be able to support. In a new paper , we used teams of Gemini 4 agents to improve well-known quantum algorithms, creating highly efficient quantum circuits. These optimized circuits, which are instructions for how a quantum computer should carry out an algorithm, could one day help us run simulations that solve complex scientific challenges, from fusion energy to drug design. To help the community build on this work, we are open-sourcing our Lean library , problem specifications, and verified solutions on GitHub. Because we cannot test resource-intensive quantum circuits on classical computers or today's small quantum processors, we have to prove that they work mathematically. Our agent teams proved each result using Lean, a formal theorem prover. Improving quantum algorithms using agentic teams For each problem, we tasked separate, independent agent teams with finding algorithmic improvements. These ideas were then verified with Lean, before entering a shared notebook. Every four hours, agents from each team met at a virtual conference to trade, debate and compare ideas. As teams produced more effective ideas over time, the computational cost gradually fell until the experiment finished. We chose to focus on applications that could one day impact some of humanity’s greatest challenges, such as clean energy and drug design, but our method is not limited to these problem areas. Running these algorithms in scientific simulations would still demand more computational resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers are likely to provide, but these improvements are significant. story|title:fork linux desktops in 139ms.content_excerpt: Host daemon for the Drums shared runtime: many isolated Linux desktops per server, with CRIU restore, fork and reset, for computer-use RL The host daemon of the Drums shared runtime: hundreds of isolated Linux desktops on one server, restored from CRIU checkpoints, forked and reset without a reboot, with a gate report and a reward audit on every episode. Training a computer-use agent needs thousands of isolated desktops, and the usual answer is one virtual machine per desktop, each booting its own kernel, operating system and applications. Drums takes a different route: one Linux host runs one booted desktop image, and every environment is a private copy-on-write state on top of it (its own overlay root, its own pid, mount, network, ipc, uts and user namespaces, its own cgroup). An environment is not booted; it is restored from a CRIU checkpoint of a running desktop, so a reset or a fork brings up Chrome, LibreOffice or GIMP where they were, in seconds, and many environments share the image's pages. drumsd is the daemon that owns those environments on a host. It creates, resets, saves (captures), forks (branches), quarantines and destroys them; drives the Drums fork of CRIU ( drums-criu , one template server per checkpoint); runs every episode behind a set of gates (restore fidelity, isolation, cgroup limits, OOM kills, application crashes) so a trainer never sees a reward from a broken desktop; and audits each reward (a second checker run, a redundant checker, a file-scope scan). It serves an HTTP API on the host that the Python SDK ( drums-sdk ), the Drums gateway and the MCP server talk to. One host serves one tenant. Environments on a host are separated from each other by namespaces, cgroups and per-env uid ranges; customers are separated from each other by virtual machines. See Security . story|title:from spectrum to structure i.content_excerpt: Robert Brunck, Stefan Ganscha, Swaroop Guntupalli, Dariusz Lasecki, Gabriella Marfani, Jack Mason, Hussain Masoom, Rose Mirshafian, Eliseo Papa and Zoi Tsangalidou Built in collaboration with analytical chemists and using community-developed tools, Mass Spec Skills empowers scientists using Google Antigravity to interpret tandem mass spectra, lay out chemical evidence, and match frontier-level retrieval accuracy even with a lightweight model. Every sample of blood, soil or plant tissue contains a vast array of small molecules, such as nutrients, hormones, drugs and their breakdown products, pollutants, or bioactive compounds with therapeutic potential. A modern mass spectrometer can detect tens of thousands of these molecular signals in a single drop of sample extract, measuring the masses of charged molecules and, in tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), the fragments they break into. These measurements, however, do not directly reveal the molecular structure. Researchers cannot immediately tell which compound produced a signal and relate it to its biological role or downstream use cases. To fully map the diversity of small molecules, which remains largely uncharted, researchers need ways to translate mass spectra to molecular structures at scale. The standard approach is to match each spectrum against reference spectra from previously measured molecules. Yet even after a decade of expanding reference libraries, spectral searches annotate on average only about 5% of measured spectra, and 10% for human samples; the rest has been called the "dark matter" of mass spectrometry. Many of the molecules producing these unannotated signals are already listed in public chemical databases, but their spectra have not been recorded, so there is no reference spectrum to compare against. Elucidating them instead requires inferring the structure directly from the observed fragment ions. Analytical chemists have a well-tested, step-by-step workflow for narrowing down candidate structures from tandem (MS/MS) spectra: check spectral reference libraries, find the molecular formula and retrieve candidate structures from chemical databases, and then test every candidate against observed fragment peaks. A coding agent writes the code, writes the tests, runs the tests and then tells you they pass. In the context of competition, the agent is the contestant, the organiser and the scoreboard all at once. Machine learning ran into this a long time ago and settled on a fix. On Kaggle you tune against a public leaderboard you can see, and you are ranked on a private one you can't. Nobody gets to report their own accuracy, because a score you can see is a score you can tune to. I was curious and experimented that on coding agents. In practice that is a handful of separate model sessions. One writes public tests from a spec. Another writes hidden tests from the same spec. A third writes a reference implementation, and any hidden test that doesn't pass on it gets thrown away. Then the implementing agent works in a sandbox where it can't read the hidden suite, and the hidden suite decides whether the work is accepted. None of it is new. It is a holdout set. It is Goodhart's law. It is the QA team writing the acceptance tests so that developers don't mark their own homework. Two things made me want to revisit it anyway. The first is that "all tests pass" has become the main thing we accept from an agent, and it comes from the party that wrote the tests. We wouldn't take that from a contractor, and we don't take it in an ML paper. The second is price. Separation of duties used to cost a second team. An independent test writer now costs a few dollars and under half an hour. There was also a question I couldn't answer in advance, and it turned out to be the one that mattered. Koi treats every deployment it runs as an experiment that explains why it performed as it did, and uses that answer for every job it plans next. H100, A100 and RTX PRO 6000 GPUs in three Google Cloud regions; 25 online and batch workloads over ten models. Every planner gets the same snapshots, catalog, checks and language model. 1.18× the goodput of the strongest baseline (OpenEvolve) at 20% lower cost per token. Goodput counts only output that meets its SLO. The ablation is a 3-hour simulation: a GPT-5.6 planner with no tools and no memory across ticks gets 71% less goodput than Koi. Koi loses 44% when it stops learning from new runs, and 39% without its causal graph. In 400- and 800-GPU simulations, Koi improves goodput by up to 45% and lowers cost per token by up to 31%. A fixed rule repeats its mistakes. Koi learns from every job, acts on rising SLO risk, and tries what it is unsure about. How a job is deployed decides its throughput and cost, for a given workload (here, 2,048-token prompts and 512-token outputs). A planner must choose this for every job at once, mostly for deployments it has never run. (Yes, the A10G is an old GPU, but the same idea holds on newer GPUs too!) Search methods keep only the end-to-end score. Koi also measures what limits each deployment. story|title:measuring and mitigating age.content_excerpt: TL;DR: AI agents often work inside a sandbox, an isolated environment that limits the files, tools, and networks they can reach. But sandboxes are sometimes insecure in ways that are hard to anticipate, and an agent that finds a way out can reach the public internet or data it wasn’t meant to see. This matters more as models become more capable, because they get better at finding ways out and can take more serious actions once outside. To understand what models do when they escape a sandbox and why, we built Siren, a new evaluation that gives them routine tasks in intentionally weakened sandboxes, with something outside the sandbox that would help them finish the task. In these deliberately tempting scenarios, recent Claude models reach outside in a fifth to a third of cases, but go on to behave in misaligned ways far less often than earlier models. We now run Siren on new Claude models before deployment, to help us identify potentially concerning behaviors and decide what to address. In this post, we explain how Siren works, report results across Claude models, and share simple deployment-time mitigations that reduce how often models reach outside by up to 96%. We also used Siren to test and tune another mitigation, auto mode, which checks agents’ actions before they run in many of our products. AI agents now routinely operate with substantial access to real software systems, running commands, editing code, and calling APIs. Each permission we give an agent makes it more useful but also increases the potential repercussions if the agent makes a mistake. To contain this risk, agents are increasingly run inside a sandbox , an isolated environment that walls the agent off from the rest of the system and the public internet. This makes the security of the sandbox critical. A poorly secured sandbox can give an agent a way to access material it was not meant to have. Depending on the weakness, the agent might be able to see or use highly sensitive tools and data, or interact with external systems through the internet. If the agent were to make a mistake or act against the user’s wishes, the consequences could be serious. Insecure sandboxes generally fall into two categories: misconfigurations and vulnerabilities. story|title:migrating our messages api t.content_excerpt: Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work. But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite , and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that covers everything . Without a reliable way to check Claude’s work, the migration of a live system is hard to trust—however quickly Claude can generate the code for it. We ran into this problem when we migrated our Messages API from Python to Rust. This API is the primary way that customers—as well as our own apps, like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew roughly 1,800 times. Rust would allow us to use far less CPU per request. Claude wrote a first version of the API’s core request path in about a week. But building trust in the migration required us to find a way to verify that our Rust API was at parity with our production API. This proved hard for several reasons, including that the Python API continued changing throughout the migration, so parity was a moving target; Claude can reply nondeterministically to the same request, so a difference between two outputs didn’t necessarily mean a bug; and we couldn't read customer requests, so we weren't able to easily see where the two versions diverged. In this post, we share how we turned the production Messages API itself into a verifier—and how that helped us test the new Rust version on production traffic, find where it differed, and automatically dispatch agents to fix those differences. This allowed us to ship an API on Rust that uses about 70% less CPU per request and cuts median time to first token by about 20% without ever taking the service offline or freezing feature development. It also measures CPU and memory of a whole process tree. It only observes : it never clicks, types or moves the mouse. The agent acts with its own tools, then uses sightline to check the result. story|title:stop paying an llm to re pla.content_excerpt: Your AI agent does a job once. Hotpath runs it every day after, as checked code, for a fraction of the model cost. This page is for everyone: the first half is plain English, the second half is for developers. Hotpath is free and open source (Apache-2.0), runs on your own machine, and needs no account. More and more teams use AI agents for jobs they do every day: writing the morning report, sorting the support inbox, checking invoices against payments, posting the weekly numbers. The agent does these jobs well. But it does them from scratch every time . Every morning it thinks again about which tools to call, in which order, and what to do with the results, even though the answer is the same as yesterday. You pay a frontier model for that thinking on every single run. Think of a new employee doing a task for the first time. They work it out, then write down the steps. From then on they follow the checklist, use their judgment only where it is needed, and ask their manager when something unusual happens. Measured on our own benchmark tasks (synthetic data, small samples; every run and every failure is published in BENCHMARK.md ): What that means for a bill: if a job runs 1,000 times a day, the Sonnet agent costs about $537 a month and the replay about $18 (or about $71 if one run in ten has to go back to the agent). Your jobs will differ: measure one before you trust any number, including ours. Where it does not help: jobs that are different every time (open research, one-off questions). Hotpath saves money on the part of your agent's work that repeats. Honest limits: a replay is only as good as its recording, so record with a capable agent. On a small free 1.7B model doing everything, recording included, 54% of 99 runs passed (87% where the recording was good). Ask your coding agent. Open Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in your agent's repository and paste this: Or measure it yourself. If you already export traces, npx @hotpathrun/cli scan reads them on your machine and shows which runs repeat and what you would save, without sending anything anywhere. See SCAN.md . A compiled workflow is a JSON file you can read, diff, review and commit. hotpath show lists its steps and hotpath view draws it as a graph. Any OpenAI-compatible API works for the models, including Ollama on your own machine. The agent (used to record and on fallback) and the replay model are set separately. story|title:the agent lake.content_excerpt: The trace of an agent is the system of record of what the agent did. It contains rich information about user intent, agent trajectory, and final outcome achieved. The simplest way to use these traces is as a debugging tool to visualize the sequence of steps an LLM application took and determine what went wrong. As agent traces become longer (as agents become more powerful) and more plentiful (as agents reach production), this manual debugging no longer scales. In order to use this trace data to drive continuous improvement of agents at scale, you need two things: We’ve been working on both of these for nearly two years. The first big piece we launched was SmithDB , a purpose-built database for traces. Over the past few months, we’ve been increasing our focus on “intelligent compute”. The reason you need “intelligent compute” is that these agent traces themselves are traces of unstructured reasoning, so intelligence is required to analyze them. In traditional data engineering, a data lake stores a shared corpus of data that different engines can query and process. As we’ve built LangSmith, we’ve noticed our platform architecture converging to that as well: a shared corpus of agent data (stored in SmithDB) with many different forms of “intelligent compute” running over it. Traditional data lakes like Snowflake and Databricks don’t have storage or “intelligent compute” optimized for this agent data. As more and more of the data a company generates becomes agent traces, we think it is important to develop this new type of platform. Most of what lands in the agent lake is traces. A trace records every step of an agent run, from the user’s input through each model call and tool call to the final output, and multi-turn conversations are grouped into threads so the whole interaction can be read together. Our agent lake, LangSmith, ingests traces from billions of agent runs per month. Some customers, like Clay, send us hundreds of millions of events per day. This kind of scale is why we built SmithDB , which is the industry’s most performant database specifically for real-time workloads on top of agent trace data. The agent lake also holds outcomes. Traces show you how the agent worked; outcomes show you the impact of that work. There are two dimensions on which to think about outcomes. First is how outcomes map to threads and/or traces . story|title:three llm inflection points.content_excerpt: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. story|title:why supervision does not sca.content_excerpt: Every agent you add is one more thing that can stop you in the middle of a thought. Managing multiple AI coding agents comes down to deciding, before the work starts, what is allowed to stop you. Name the few moments that need a person. Everything else the agent settles alone, or it writes down what it needs and waits for you. Then what waits sits in one list, and you read it when you choose. Addy Osmani put the limit in one sentence in 2026. "What scales is your throughput of supervision, not your throughput of understanding." He gives his own number too. "My ceiling for a typical session is somewhere around three to four threads depending on complexity." His advice is to narrow each agent's task before you cut the count. We agree. He also writes that an agent's judgment calls cannot queue up like email, and there we part. They cannot queue when any agent may ask anything at any time. They can when the flow says in advance which questions exist. Tillerly runs AI coding agents on your team's machines, sandboxed, from ticket to pull request. Every ticket takes the same seven Steps, plan, publish, resolve, pull request, CI, QA and merge, and each Step blocks the next. One agent, the planner, designs the change. Another, the resolver, implements it. A person is needed at a short, fixed list of moments. Outside that list an agent has two choices. Settle it, or write down what it needs and wait. The Builder and its seven Steps says what each Step does. The resolver implements the ticket in its own worktree, runs your repository's checks, and pushes the ticket's branch. None of that asks you anything. Review works the same way, when the project's Follow comments setting is on. Within a few minutes of a new comment on the pull request, the resolver reads it and fixes what it can prove. A comment that comes while the build is red starts a fix of the build instead. It leaves you the reply, ready to paste. A comment it cannot settle waits for you. Each thing an agent needs from you becomes a human action. Open a pull request, reply to a reviewer, groom and start a bug, take a decision. They are all listed on Work, the dashboard's home. Every open one is listed, none behind a second page, and the same open item is never added twice. So three agents asking are not three terminals to watch. story|variant:mini,pro|title:hill climbi.content_excerpt: Inkling 2 Mini came out last week and sets a new state of the art for local AI and smaller open-source models. With ~26B total parameters (3B active per token), multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window, it leads its weight class on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 and across 32 of 48 benchmarks against models like Gemma 4 31B and Qwen3.8-27B, making it a strong open option for coding, tool use, and reasoning on modest hardware. We wrote an extensive blog post on how you can use it within the Hugging Face ecosystem here . One of the interesting aspects of Inkling 2 Mini that might explain its great performance is its unusual architecture. Inkling 2 Mini is a looped Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model with 24 physical layers where the middle 12 layers run three times, so every token passes through 48 layers. The checkpoint ships in mixed NVFP4 and MXFP8 and bundles a DSpark drafter for speculative decoding. Both vLLM and SGLang, the go-to frameworks for LLM inference, support it on nightly builds, though the published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200 and GB300 GPUs ( sm100 ), leaving out sm120 cards like the NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 where kernel compatibility can differ. We wanted to see how fast we could serve it on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 96 GB, the GPU behind an nvidia-rtx-pro-6000 Inference Endpoint . Rather than tuning flags by hand, we gave a coding agent the inference-optimisation skill, the hf CLI, and access to Hugging Face Jobs , and let it run experiments for an afternoon. Across 46 valid benchmark runs, single-user decode went from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%) (ahead of the 167.7 tok/s community SGLang + DSpark benchmark on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU) and 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding. Greedy outputs are byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passes 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest.
